title: The autopsy
lede: Tap a cause to see the evidence. The percentages are our editorial weighting. The evidence under each one is sourced.

causes.title: Expansion into weak sites
causes.text: General Foods took about 700 units to 1,200 outlets in roughly three years and made “inflated property commitments in weak marketing areas.” The result was an $83 million loss and a planned 25% cut in the chain.[^1]

causes.title: A packaged-goods owner running restaurants
causes.text: Management turnover was “nearly total” within two years of the purchase, and General Foods filled the gaps with its own people. Its president lost his job over the result.[^1] Time adds an ill-judged logo redesign.[^4]

causes.title: Rivals with more scale
causes.text: McDonald’s went from 1,000 restaurants in 1968 to 4,177 in 1976, while Burger Chef shrank.[^4][^20] Burger King grew from 274 stores in 1967 to 3,500 in 1982, and Wendy’s from one restaurant to 1,767 in ten years.[^21][^22]

causes.title: A decade without a settled identity
causes.text: One local history counts four different logos and store designs during the 1970s.[^9] Innovations such as the Funmeal and the Works Bar were real but were copied by larger chains.[^6][^17]

causes.title: An owner that wanted out
causes.text: By 1981 the chain was “barely a breakeven operation,” and General Foods said it was “not central to the long-term direction” of the company. The buyer wanted locations for Hardee’s, not a second brand.[^2][^3][^10]

disclaimer: the weights are an interpretive model by the Spectre Brands editors, not a measured quantity. Burger Chef’s own accounts were never public, so the evidence is what General Foods told the press and what later histories recorded.
